Learn Brief in Y Minutes

Brief is a strict markup language designed to replace Markdown for documents written by humans and consumed by humans and LLMs. It has three goals:

  1. One way to do it. Every construct has a single canonical spelling.

    Ambiguous input is a compile error, not a guess.

  2. Token economy. The source and the rendered LLM output are designed

    to be cheaper than equivalent Markdown.

  3. Real compiler. Errors come with source spans, error codes, and help

    text, like rustc. There are no warnings — just success or failure.

There is no inline HTML. The single extension point is shortcodes.

The whole language fits in one file. Read it top to bottom.

1. Comments

Line comments start with // and must occupy the whole line. They are stripped before any output.

Block comments use C-style /* */ delimiters. They cannot nest, and the opening /* and closing */ must each appear at the start or end of a line — never in the middle of text.

2. Headings

Brief supports six levels of headings, written with # through ######, followed by exactly one space and the heading text.

# Heading level 1
## Heading level 2
### Heading level 3
#### Heading level 4
##### Heading level 5
###### Heading level 6

Seven or more # is an error: B0301 "heading level exceeds maximum of 6". Setext headings (=== / --- underlines) do NOT exist. Two spaces, zero spaces, or no text after the # run are all errors.

3. Paragraphs and line breaks

Multiple consecutive non-blank lines that don't begin with a block sigil get joined with a single space when rendered. A blank line separates paragraphs. A trailing backslash at the end of a line is the hard-break marker — it forces a line break inside a single paragraph.

This is one paragraph
that spans two lines.

This is the next paragraph.\
And this line breaks within it.

4. Inline emphasis

Each kind of emphasis uses a SINGLE-character marker on each side:

  • *bold* renders as strong
  • _italic_ renders as em
  • +underline+ renders as underline
  • ~strike~ renders as strikethrough

Doubled markers (**bold**, __italic__) are NOT valid. Brief refuses them rather than treating them as a different style — this is the entire point.

A line with *bold*, _italic_, +underline+, and ~strikethrough~ words.

*bold with _italic inside_ and back to bold*

Emphasis kinds nest freely with each other, but the SAME kind cannot nest (that would be B0204). Multi-line emphasis is also an error (B0205).

A marker flanked by alphanumerics on both sides is treated as a literal character, not as emphasis:

snake_case_name              // literal — no italic
file_with_underscores.txt    // literal
3*4 = 12                     // literal asterisks

To force a marker to be literal in a position where it would otherwise be emphasis, escape it with \:

This costs \*5\* dollars.

5. Inline code

Use the printf function. To include a literal backtick inside inline code, switch to the double-backtick form. This is the ONLY exception in the whole language to the "one canonical form" rule, and it exists because you cannot escape inside a verbatim region.

Run ``echo `whoami` `` to print the user.

6. Lists

Two kinds — unordered and ordered — and they do NOT mix at the same level. Switching between them ends the previous list.

The unordered marker is - followed by exactly one space. * and + are NOT valid unordered markers.

- first item
- second item
- third item

The ordered marker is digits, then ., then exactly one space. Numbering MUST be sequential starting from 1. Out-of-order is an error (B0501) — the renderer does not silently renumber for you.

1. step one
2. step two
3. step three

Nested lists use exactly TWO spaces of indentation per level. One space, three spaces, or tabs are all errors.

- top level
  - nested
    - deeper still
  - back to nested
- another top

You can mix list types between levels:

1. ordered top
  - bullet inside
  - another bullet
2. ordered top again

A list item can have continuation lines, indented to match the content column (the marker plus its space):

- this item has
  a continuation line
- next item

Unordered list items can carry a task-state marker as their first content. The marker is exactly [x] (done) or [ ] (todo) — strict literal: lowercase x, single space inside the brackets, single space after. Anything else (uppercase X, [ ] with two spaces, [x] without a trailing space) is plain text.

- [x] ship v0.4
- [ ] write release notes
- plain bullet, not a task

HTML emit renders these as a checkbox <input type="checkbox" disabled> inside <li class="task-list-item">, with the parent <ul> carrying

class="contains-task-list" if any item is a task. LLM emit preserves the marker verbatim. Task markers are NOT supported on ordered list items — 1. [x] foo is just text.

7. Blockquotes

A blockquote starts with > followed by exactly one space. Subsequent lines beginning the same way continue it. Nested blockquotes use additional > markers. A blank line ends the blockquote.

> An outer quote.
>> A nested quote.
> Back to the outer.

8. Code blocks

Triple-backtick fences only. Tilde fences (~~~) and four-space-indent code blocks are NOT supported. The opening fence may include a language tag. Content between the fences is verbatim — no escaping, no inline parsing. Unterminated fences are an error (B0305) at end of file.

For example, here is a real fenced Rust block:

fn main() {
    println!("hi");
}

9. Horizontal rule

Exactly three dashes, on a line by themselves. Two or four dashes are errors.

10. Tables

Tables are introduced by the @t directive. The first |-row is the header. There is NO separator row.

NameAgeCity
John30NYC
Jane25LA

The trailing | is optional. Cells are trimmed of leading and trailing whitespace. Every row must have the same number of cells as the header — mismatches are an error (B0502).

Column alignment is set on the directive:

NameScoreStatus
Ada1024active
Bob42idle

Alignment array length must match the column count (B0504).

11. Shortcodes — the single extension point

Shortcodes are how Brief replaces inline HTML. Two forms exist: an inline form @name(args)[content] and a block form that opens with

@name(args), has a body, and closes with @end.

Arguments inside (...) are positional or keyword (mixed allowed, positionals first). Argument values are bare idents, integers, double-quoted strings, or arrays. The [content] of an inline shortcode is parsed as inline. Block bodies are parsed as full blocks (recursively). All shortcodes must be REGISTERED — using an unknown one is an error (B0401).

Built-in shortcodes that ship with the reference compiler:

NameFormPurpose
linkinlinehyperlink
imageinlineimage
kbdinlinekeyboard input
subinlinesubscript (replaces inline <sub>)
supinlinesuperscript (replaces inline <sup>)
detailsblockcollapsible block (replaces <details>/<summary>)
tblocktables (special-cased)
codeblocksame as triple-backtick fence
calloutblockboxed note
mathbothLaTeX math, inline or block
footnoteinlinefootnote text

Inline HTML has no general escape hatch in Brief. The four built-ins above (@kbd, @sub, @sup, @details) cover the inline tags that came up most often in real documents. @br is not provided — use \ at end of line (§12) for hard breaks. Anything else means the document shouldn't be inline-HTML in the first place; if you must, register a custom shortcode in brief.toml.

An inline link — note the markdown-style [text](url) sugar that supplies the URL as positional arg #1:

See the spec for details.

An image with required keyword args (inline, embedded in a paragraph):

The architecture is shown here: .

Keyboard input: press Ctrl+C to abort.

Inline math: the energy is E = m c^2.

A footnote: this claim is contested.1 The inline form is the only form — definitions live in the [...] body next to the reference, never elsewhere in the file. The compiler auto-numbers them in document order and emits a list at the end (HTML <ol class="footnotes">, LLM [^1]: ...).

A block callout — the kind argument is constrained to one of info,

warning, or danger; anything else is B0404 BadEnumValue.

Watch out for the Shift+Delete shortcut on Linux. It can wipe data without going through the trash.

Custom shortcodes are registered in brief.toml (see §13). User-defined shortcodes can NEVER be self-terminating — only @t and the triple-backtick fence are allowed that special form.

12. Escapes

\ escapes the next character, treating it as a literal. \\ produces a literal backslash. Escapes are honored everywhere EXCEPT inside code spans and code blocks, which are verbatim by definition.

\*not bold\* \[not a bracket\] \\\\backslash

13. Compiling

brief compile doc.brf --target=html
brief compile doc.brf --target=llm --report-tokens
brief compile doc.brf --target=json

The --target=llm mode produces a deterministic, token-minimized rendering for inclusion in LLM prompts. Comments are stripped, blank lines are collapsed, indentation drops to one space per level, emphasis markers are preserved (use --strip-emphasis to drop them), and shortcodes render to compact forms:

  • @link[text](url) becomes [text](url)
  • @image(src, alt) becomes [image: alt] (--keep-asset-urls preserves the URL)
  • @callout(kind: warning) ... becomes [!warning] ... [/!]
  • @math[x^2] becomes $x^2$
  • @footnote[body] becomes [^N] inline; definitions are appended at

    the end of the document as [^N]: body lines

--report-tokens prints a stderr line with a cl100k character/token estimate. The estimate is best-effort and not normative.

14. Configuration: brief.toml

At the project root, place a brief.toml. It declares custom shortcodes, enables strictness flags, and points to templates.

[project]
name = "my-docs"
version = "0.1.0"

[compile]
strict_heading_levels = true
default_target = "html"

[shortcodes.note]
kind = "block"
template_html = "<aside class=\"note\">{{content}}</aside>"
template_llm = "[note] {{content}} [/note]"

[shortcodes.callout]
kind = "block"
arguments = { kind = { type = "string", required = true,
  oneof = ["info", "warning", "danger"] } }
template_html = "templates/callout.html"

Templates are minimal mustache: only {{content}} (rendered children) and {{args.name}} (argument values). No conditionals, no loops, no embedded code. Logic belongs in build hooks, not templates.

15. Diagnostics and error codes

Errors come out in rustc form:

error[B0204]: emphasis cannot nest with the same marker
  --> doc.brf:14:23
   |
14 | This is *outer *inner* outer*.
   |        ^^^^^^^ inner emphasis re-uses the `*` marker
   |
   = help: use a different emphasis marker for the inner span,
           e.g. _outer *inner* outer_

Code ranges:

  • B01xx — lexical (tabs, BOM, encoding)
  • B02xx — inline parsing (emphasis, code spans)
  • B03xx — block parsing (headings, fences, comments)
  • B04xx — shortcode resolution (unknown, type, enum, form)
  • B05xx — semantic / cross-cutting (list sequence, table columns)

brief explain B0204 prints the long-form explanation. There is no

--allow-warnings. There never will be.

16. The whole list of things that are intentionally NOT here

  • Inline HTML — use a shortcode.
  • **bold** / __italic__ — one marker on each side; period.
  • * or + for bullets — only - is valid.
  • Setext headings — only #-prefixed.
  • Indented code blocks — use triple-backtick fences.
  • Reference-style links — use @link[text](url).
  • Table separator row — @t header is implicit.
  • Renumbering ordered lists — 1, 2, 3 or it's an error.
  • Tab characters anywhere — two-space indent only.
  • Inline trailing comments — comments are whole lines.

If a thing isn't on this page, it isn't in the language.
